rv.q: It has much of what Broadway lovers would want from such a musical, including songs by Kander and Ebb
It has much of what Broadway lovers would want from such a musical, including songs by Kander and Ebb plus half a dozen more written for the show by Kander in collaboration with Miranda.
The production gets wooden when Oscar goes on long rants that are thinly veiled exposition, catching the audience up on every nook and cranny of his career.
Even the rosiest-hued urban utopia can get a bit tiresome when it’s this overstuffed with good intentions.
It feels like all of the writers got to do their thing and make their points, but no one insisted on everyone getting on board with the same style and story.
The show has moments of real beauty and excitement, but they're too often buried under the weight of a sprawling, unfocused book
The result is a run-of-the-mill big Broadway extravaganza that knows where, but not when, it is.

Among the new songs, Kander and Miranda share credit on six, with the ebullient opening number Cheering for Me Now and hopeful love song Can You Hear Me? But the pieces de résistance, two numbers that Liza Minnelli sung in the film, are turned into showstoppers by Uzele: the fiery ballad But the World Goes ’Round and the unforgettable title song...
But they are sewn together, by book writer David Thompson and co-writer Sharon Washington, with narrative threads too flimsy to keep them attached to each other or to us.
For all the musical’s insistence on the city’s vitality, it’s glassy-eyed and complacent.
And sadly, none make much of an impression, mired as they are in a syrupy muck of good sentiments and grating civic cheerleading.
The fake poetry of it all becomes cloying, even for a native New Yorker who has sentimental leanings in this direction.
They paint a city of pink sunsets and bland cliches.
It’s tired, sappy and deathly dull.
With “New York, New York” – the BEST is what is delivered.
I’ll only say it’s the most exhilarating finale I can remember ever experiencing on a Broadway stage.

Each minute of New York, New York is buzzing with life, as background dancers and actors flit in and out of view, telling clever little visual stories, giving New York, New York the energy of its titular city.
By the end of the show, the audience has submitted to the pizzazzy uplift.
However, even with “additional lyrics” by wunderkind Lyn
“New York, New York,” under the savvy direction and choreography of Susan Stroman and featuring a score by John Kander and the late Fred Ebb, additional lyrics by Lin

In the last few minutes, as the orchestra rises from the pit and Uzele commands the stage as if performing for a sold-out audience at Radio City Music Hall, all of the production's flaws, missed opportunities, and dashed dreams of another classic Kander and Ebb musical are almost forgiven.

While it removes the abusive relationship between Jimmy and Francine from the film, in doing so it waters down the story to a rather old-fashioned “newcomers make good in the big city” tale we have seen before.
Like the city it’s named after, “New York, New York” is full of promise and potential – neither of which is completely fulfilled.
But this can only go so far, and it’s not long before New York, New York starts to feel like a Radio City Music Hall pageant rather than an actual book musical.
A lot of money must have gone into this physically elaborate, but frequently disappointing, effort, a kind of sloppy wet kiss to the immediate postwar years of 1946-1947.
Unfortunately for New York, New York, now running on Broadway at the St. James Theatre, there isn’t much else.
It is also an overstuffed misfire.

Very little feels original in New York, New York; instead, this musical, directed and choreographed by Susan Stroman, feels like a reheated casserole of so many other romanticized New York narratives, stereotypes, and well-worn signifiers.
They’re stuck in a barebones boy-meets-girl scenario that doesn’t allow for any real emotional investment.
The show catches fire for the final half-hour, culminating in a coup de théâtre leading into a smashing rendition of the title song every bit as exciting as you’d find in a prime nitery.

New York, New York, accomplishes the near impossible, delivering wide-eyed optimism with an American Dream reality check, all wrapped up in a beautiful package that will appeal to first-time visitors as well as jaded locals who wonder why they put up with the city that never sleeps.
As a New Yorker, I found New York, New York dazzling and enchanting.
The biggest problem is that the show is that it is dull.
This fabulous Big Broadway Musical soars to unimaginable new heights

cn.t: Critics find this Kander and Ebb musical a well-intentioned but overstuffed love letter to NYC that struggles with an unfocused book, though Stroman's choreography and production values occasionally dazzle.

sg.ra: Rows B-L are the house's actual sweet-spot band — Row A loses legroom and cranes necks because the St. James stage is raised on multiple recent productions (Sunset's LED wall, Something Rotten!'s set), while Row L is the last row before both the shallow rake AND the mezzanine overhang bite into the view Rows M+ hit the St. James's signature rake-and-overhang double-whammy — shorter patrons report 'craning around heads' and top-of-stage cutoff; a below-average experience for a 1,710-seat house

The Row D aisle-angled seats (D1/D2) are a genuine St. James unicorn — the row is set at a different angle than the rows in front so no seat sits directly ahead of you; this bypasses the flat-rake problem that defines the rest of the house 'Partial view' labeled seats in rows A-C side orchestra are heavily production-dependent — Into The Woods and Sunset (downstage-centric) work fine; Frozen's left-side set wall and Something Rotten!'s spread staging defeat them Back rows Q-S side orchestra sit directly under the mezzanine overhang — OK view of downstage action but top-of-set elements (screens, signage) cut off

Front mezzanine (Row A) is frequently called the best seat in the 1,710-seat house — Wikipedia notes the mezz 'extends over what were originally the tenth row of orchestra seats,' so you're unusually close for an upper tier, and because the orchestra's rake is so shallow, veterans repeatedly prefer Row A mezz to mid-orchestra at this specific house Row A has two specific St. James quirks that are production-sensitive — a low brass railing and an extension lighting rig on the mezz front; fine for average height but shorter patrons hit them, and Sunset Boulevard's onstage-lip blocking can make Row A worse than Row B-C

Front rows A-C side mezzanine are the house's best discount — St. James veterans (Patash: 'Gypsy, Bullets Over Broadway, A Funny Thing Happened... my favorite seats... I don't mind the side section in the least') buy them deliberately over pricier orchestra for every major musical High-seat-number side mezz (>18 in rows B-F) hits the mezzanine curvature problem — not just off-angle but the row pitches away from the stage creating sub-inch knee clearance Row B seat 18 area (where pricing typically breaks to a cheaper bracket) is a genuine value sweet spot — view is nearly identical to Row A but noticeably cheaper; confirmed across multiple productions

Rear mezz is the house's classic value trap — priced as mezzanine but the rake flattens and you're a third of the way back in a 1,710-seat house; reviewers describe needing seat boosters and sliding to the seat edge to see anything. Row Q aisle has an additional specific quirk: a corridor-exit light stays on during the show. Row J is the one exception in the rear-mezz block — it's the first row of a rear bank with a walkway in front, so no heads block the view; veterans specifically target it as the discount version of front mezz

Row A center balcony is the upper-tier's saving grace — BWW veterans split sharply (one calls it 'one of the worst balconies on Broadway', others swear by it), but the consensus lands on Row A specifically because the no-lean position, sound improvement from the extra speaker truss, and low railing make it better than rear mezz for the same price The balcony is a physical climb — 'like climbing a tower' — and is the second balcony; older patrons or anyone with mobility should not attempt at this house specifically Row A is the ONLY row that reliably clears the railing — behind Row A the rail bisects the stage; chain-reaction lean-forward effect forces everyone below to follow suit

Side balcony behind Row A combines every St. James hazard in one seat — side-angle, railing blocking downstage, second-balcony height, tight legroom, and (per multiple patrons) lottery-only sales because the house knows they're problematic Row A side balcony aisle seats (1-3 L, 2-4 R) are the one exception — sightlines avoid the railing, you're 'almost right over the front of the mezzanine,' and legroom is usable; anything behind Row A or away from the aisle is genuinely skip-tier at this house because back side-balcony also carries sound-mix issues off-axis from the speaker truss
